about: The Epistle of the feast of the Most Holy Body of Christ, 1 Corinthians 11:23–29. Saint Paul hands on the institution of the Eucharist and warns against receiving the Lord’s Body and Blood unworthily.

seg.tr: Brothers: For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: the Lord Jesus, on the night when He was betrayed, took bread and, giving thanks, broke it and said: “Take and eat: this is My Body, which will be given up for you. Do this in remembrance of Me.”
Likewise, after supper He also took the chalice, saying: “This chalice is the new covenant in My Blood. Do this, whenever you drink, in remembrance of Me.”

ex.w044: The chalice is the object of an understood “took.” The same action was stated explicitly with the bread: “accépit panem.”

seg.tr: For whenever you eat this bread and drink the chalice, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.

ex.w069: The chalice is the object of “bibétis,” which follows it: “you drink the chalice.” The Latin places the object before the verb.

seg.tr: Therefore, whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s chalice unworthily will be guilty of an offense against the Lord’s Body and Blood.

a.g: will be guilty of an offense

ex.w086: “Reus” takes the genitives “córporis et sánguinis”: the guilt concerns an offense against the Lord’s Body and Blood. It does not mean that the Body and Blood are guilty. “Indígne” describes the unworthy manner of receiving.

seg.tr: But let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink from the chalice.

a.g: But let a person examine himself

seg.tr: For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself, without discerning the Lord’s Body.

ex.w112: Eating and drinking “judgment on himself” expresses the consequence of receiving unworthily. “Iudícium” here denotes adverse judgment. The word alone does not specify eternal damnation.
